title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Power
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: A cyberattack has kept a Chilean solar-and-battery plant off the grid for almost three months, and no one has said which control systems were hit
items.content_text: Chile’s National Electric Coordinator still lists the 103 MW Huatacondo solar plant in Tarapacá, and its 98 MW / 312 MWh battery system, at zero availability in its 14 November report, recorded as a forced outage caused by a cyberattack. The coordinator activated its disconnection protocol on 27 August after the company reported the incident; T13 dates the attack to 26 August. The same records show a cyber-caused forced disconnection of a transformer at the Santa Rita substation that day. On 11 November a member of Congress asked which systems (SCADA, protection, inverters, battery management) were compromised and whether notification duties were met; no answer had been published by 16 November. Owner, entry route and attacker are undisclosed. A plant disconnected for safety can stay dark for months if it cannot show its control systems are clean (editorial assessment).

_otthreatfeed.category: Top Story
_otthreatfeed.source_name: ESS News / pv magazine (17 Nov 2026, citing Coordinador Eléctrico Nacional records); T13 (16 Nov 2026, in Spanish); pv magazine Latin America (16 Nov 2026, congressional requests, in Spanish)
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Ongoing — still offline per 14 Nov 2026 coordinator report; congressional requests 11 Nov 2026; reported 16–17 Nov 2026; attack 26 Aug 2026

items.title: Norway says the Equinor and Skagerak Energi intrusions came through Microsoft’s Azure API Management cloud service
items.content_text: On 23 November Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) said an unidentified actor has been stealing access tokens and other sensitive data from Microsoft Azure API Management (APIM), and that Equinor and Skagerak Energi, a power and renewables utility in eastern Norway, were among the organisations hit. Equinor detected its intrusion on 17 November and contained it by 20 November; Skagerak disclosed its attack a day later. Both say oil, gas and electricity production carried on normally. A reported, non-public Microsoft notice says an issue in older “Classic” APIM tiers was found on 18 November and the access path closed the next day; Microsoft has issued key-rotation guidance but not publicly linked it to Norway. Utilities that move metering, dispatch or market data through cloud APIs should rotate those secrets now (editorial assessment).

items.title: Peninsula Energy confirms attackers reached plant and wellfield control systems at its Wyoming uranium site, which is shut down
items.content_text: Peninsula Energy, an ASX-listed uranium producer, said on 25 November that the cyber incident found late on 20 November affected the plant and wellfield operating and control systems at its Lance in-situ recovery project in Crook County, Wyoming. The site has been shut down while the investigation continues, and the company’s shares are suspended until 30 November. Its US and Australian administrative systems were earlier reported as unaffected. Peninsula has not said how the attackers got in, what they did inside the control systems or when it expects to restart, and no group has claimed the attack. No effect on any power plant is reported. Lance produces uranium for nuclear fuel, so this is a confirmed OT shutdown in the generation fuel chain (editorial assessment).

items.title: South Korea’s state power utility KEPCO confirms about 1.5 million records stolen, as turbine maker Suzlon reports its own incident
items.content_text: Korea Electric Power Corp (KEPCO) confirmed on 22 November that an attacker got into its internal network and reached two systems: its KEPCO ON customer billing and payment platform and its supplier procurement system. It detected the intrusion on 20 November, cut external access and suspended the affected services. The company says data on about 650,000 customers, 427,000 supplier representatives and 443,000 employees was exposed, roughly 1.52 million people. It has not said how the attacker got in, and a forum actor’s 19 November claim is unverified. No effect on power supply is reported. A day later India’s Suzlon Energy disclosed a cyber incident and said business-critical applications were unaffected. Procurement systems hold supplier contacts and project details that make good phishing material for grid vendors (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers rooted unpatched Check Point gateways through PHP2Shell, planted backdoors and wiped a VMware host; the root flaw is now in KEV
items.content_text: Check Point Research said on 12 November that attackers exploited the PHP2Shell flaws on unpatched Check Point Mobile Access portals from 30 October, then used a local flaw (CVE-2026-123039) to become root. They planted backdoors, pivoted to a VMware ESXi host and ran a wiper. The first wave hit Israeli organizations, some destructively; a second wave from 2 November reached several countries without destruction. Attribution is unconfirmed (tooling resembles China-nexus UNC5221). CISA added the root flaw to KEV on 13 November. No OT victim is reported, but these firewalls often sit at the IT/OT boundary and ESXi often hosts HMIs and historians (editorial assessment).

items.title: Osaki Electric confirms data left its network and plans a staged restart of smart-meter production from 27 November
items.content_text: Osaki Electric, a Japanese smart-meter maker, found ransomware on 17 November and suspended production and shipments at its Saitama centre and two group plants. The company has said the intruder most likely got in on 15 November by password guessing against a VPN account without multi-factor authentication. In a 25 November filing it confirmed data was sent to an external destination, and set out a staged restart of production from 27 November, with shipments planned from 1 and 7 December. A Qilin leak-site claim has not been verified. Production equipment and meters already in the field are reported unaffected. For utilities the exposure is supplier-side: delayed meter rollouts and questions about the systems that build and sign device firmware (editorial assessment).

items.title: Illinois investigates an apparent cyberattack attempt on the Algonquin Dam on the Fox River
items.content_text: The Illinois Department of Natural Resources said on 20 November that it detected an apparent attempted cyberattack on the Algonquin Dam, about 45 miles northwest of Chicago, on 16 November. Staff blocked the unauthorised access at once, and the dam stayed secure and fully operational. IDNR has not said which system was targeted or whether gate controls were reachable. Illinois State Police, state agencies and CISA are investigating; no link to other attacks and no group has been named. For dam owners, hydro operators included, it is a prompt to check who can reach gate and spillway controls remotely (editorial assessment).

items.title: Lumen: Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train” relay chains have carried zero-day attacks on network-management platforms since 2023, and energy is among the targeted sectors
items.content_text: Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs published research on 28 October describing Silent Train, a framework Volt Typhoon has used since about November 2023 to reach management and control-plane systems. Each operation runs through a short-lived chain of compromised home-office routers, IoT devices and enterprise equipment that is torn down after use, which makes the source hard to trace. Lumen ties four confirmed zero-day campaigns and one likely one to the group: N-able N-central (CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876), Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN (CVE-2026-20127, CVSS v3.1 10.0, Cisco), VeloCloud Orchestrator (CVE-2026-16812) and Versa Director, with Quest KACE assessed as a likely zero-day; the CVEs it names are in KEV. These are earlier flaws than the Cisco SD-WAN Manager and VeloCloud flaws carded on this page, and Lumen does not tie those to Volt Typhoon. Black Lotus Labs says it has sent hundreds of victim notifications over about three years; named sectors include telecoms, government, defence, managed service providers and critical infrastructure in water, energy, transportation, maritime, rail, aviation and emergency services. No utility victim is named and no OT intrusion is described. Lumen advises keeping administrative interfaces off the internet, patching management and control-plane systems first and extending log retention, and points to CISA’s AA24-038A and AA26-113A. For utilities, the SD-WAN orchestrators and remote-management tools that link control centres to field sites are the kind of platform this actor goes after (editorial assessment).

items.title: DHS tells Congress Iran-backed hackers have stepped up attacks on US water, energy and transport since February, while officials rule out hacking in last week’s outages
items.content_text: In written testimony for a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on 18 November, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Iranian state-sponsored groups and pro-Iranian criminals have targeted US critical infrastructure since the conflict with Iran began in February, with transportation, healthcare, water, energy and financial services increasingly in their sights. He described the attacks so far as mostly localized, low-damage disruptions of poorly secured industrial control systems, but warned that weak systems and poor cyber hygiene could have devastating consequences. At the same hearing the Director of National Intelligence and DHS said they found no evidence that hackers caused last week’s Microsoft 365 outage, the nationwide FAA ground stop or other recent disruptions, which officials tie to software defects and upgrade failures. Separately, AttackIQ research released on 17 November describes Iranian groups handing network access to one another, with long-running espionage access later passed to teams pursuing destructive goals, sometimes disguised as ransomware or hacktivism, often reaching targets through contractors and suppliers. For OT owners, the official US view now matches France’s: Iran is going after the weakest exposed controllers.

items.title: FBI warns criminals are using an AI-driven intrusion framework, ARTEX, against energy and other critical infrastructure, and a Texas regulator tells energy firms to harden now
items.content_text: On 18 November Texas Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian urged producers, pipeline operators and energy firms to harden their defences, citing recent outages and a 13 November FBI IC3 advisory on ARTEX. The FBI describes ARTEX as an AI-driven autonomous penetration-testing framework that malicious actors have used to automate stages of an intrusion, with targets including energy, government, financial services and other critical infrastructure. Christian said ARTEX “may not be the only explanation” for the outages; no causal link has been established, and no Texas victim, incident or CVE has been named. The commission regulates oil and gas, not electricity, but the targeting applies equally to generators and transmission owners. Automated tooling shortens the time between an exposed service and an intrusion, so exposure reviews need to run continuously, not yearly (editorial assessment).

items.title: An AI-assisted crew broke into Check Point firewall management servers at more than 20 organisations, including energy companies
items.content_text: GreyNoise reported that a crew it tracks as GT13, using AI-assisted tooling, breached Check Point Security Management servers at no fewer than 22 organisations between 17 October and 2 November, with energy, transport and manufacturing among the sectors hit, according to Cybersecurity Dive on 24 November. Victims are not named and no OT impact is reported. A management server holds the policy for every gateway it controls, so whoever owns it can quietly change the rules at the IT/OT boundary. This is separate from the gateway-level PHP2Shell intrusions (see Incidents & Attacks), but it hits the same product family. Power-sector relevance is editorial assessment.

items.title: Dragos counts 1,266 ransomware attacks on industrial organizations in Q3, up 11%, and found no case of an operator touching a control system
items.content_text: Dragos said on 16 November that ransomware hit 1,266 industrial organizations between July and September 2026, up 11% on the second quarter, while the number of brands claiming industrial victims jumped from 70 to 99. Manufacturing took 69% of cases, followed by the ICS ecosystem of integrators, engineering firms and equipment makers (116) and transport and logistics (105); oil and gas logged 47. Qilin and The Gentlemen drove 29% of the total. Dragos saw no Q3 case of a ransomware operator manipulating a control system: production stopped because the IT, ERP and virtualization layers plants rely on went down, as when Fairlife reportedly halted all four of its US plants for about 11 days. Entry came through edge devices and enterprise applications exploited within days of disclosure, and through stolen VPN and firewall credentials. Check Point separately counted a record 1,063 claimed victims across all sectors in October.

items.title: Siemens adds WTV676 and WTV776 metering gateways to its PHP2Shell advisory, while parts of Spectrum Power still have no fix
items.content_text: Siemens revised SSA-166980 to V1.4 on 16 November to add its WTV676 and WTV776 metering gateways to the products affected by PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both in CISA KEV), and to V1.5 on 18 November with a fix for WTV676-HB6035: firmware FW6.9.22-3.4. WTV776-HB6035 has no fix. Grid-control parts also remain unfixed: Spectrum Power 4 with Nagios or Zabbix, Web Office Portal V3.0 to V3.2 and HISViews V1.0, plus AMIS TS and two blueplanet 360 NX3 M6 models; Energy Engage V2.0SP9 will get no fix. Spectrum Power 3 and 7 take Red Hat’s PHP patches, Spectrum Power TG needs PHP 8.5.12 and Energy Engage V3.1SP1 PHP 8.1.34 release 6. ABB lists its Netcontrol RTUs and ASPECT gateways and Schneider a Foxboro DCS server. No Siemens, ABB or Schneider product is reported exploited, but the same flaws have been used to root PAN-OS firewalls and Check Point gateways (see Incidents & Attacks), so an exposed web front end next to grid control is a real foothold (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers try to plant bots on Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 edge gateways through a CVSS 10 Node-RED flaw
items.content_text: VulnCheck reported that from 30 October attackers were trying to exploit CVE-2026-58115 against its honeypots. The flaw, rated CVSS 10.0, is missing authentication in the Node-RED HTTP interface on SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices running Industrial OS with Node-RED installed: an unauthenticated attacker can create flows that run code with maximum privileges. The first attempts deployed a flow that downloaded and ran a Linux bot; later ones used a two-stage downloader, and some added an HTTP endpoint wired to an exec node, a backdoor that survives a reboot even if a memory-resident implant is lost. Siemens published SSA-834709 in August; the fix is Node-RED 4.3.4.1 or later, or removing Node-RED. Only honeypots were hit, and no compromise of a real device has been reported. IoT2050 boxes are used as data-collection gateways at substations and generation sites, so look for ones you did not know about (editorial assessment).

items.title: A vCenter authentication bypass was exploited as a zero-day for two months before Broadcom’s 19 November patch; vCenter 7.0 gets no fix
items.content_text: Broadcom patched CVE-2026-123890 on 19 November, a critical flaw in vCenter’s directory service that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker obtain an administrator session. Google’s Mandiant, which reported the bug, says a suspected China-linked espionage group it tracks as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221, also called Warp Panda) exploited it for more than two months beforehand. In the incidents Mandiant investigated, the group got in through a BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw, moved to Linux appliances, attacked vCenter in early September with a custom tool called Bonesaw, stole SAML signing material and the vCenter master key, created an SSO admin account, forged tokens and moved on to ESXi hosts. Fixes are in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m; end-of-life vCenter 7.0 has no public patch. No victims or sectors are named. Many plants run HMIs, historians and engineering workstations as virtual machines, so whoever controls vCenter controls those hosts (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers root clustered Cisco Expressway gateways soon after a public exploit, and CISA adds the flaw to KEV
items.content_text: Security firm F6 says attackers exploited CVE-2026-76466, a critical flaw in clustered Cisco Expressway Core and Edge deployments, shortly after proof-of-concept code appeared on GitHub. They broke into two internet-facing Expressway nodes at an unnamed Russian organization, moved to two more cluster nodes inside the network, and gained root. From there they ran Python scripts, which F6 says show signs of AI-assisted writing, to scan for SMB shares, SQL Server and WinRM hosts and to search GitLab for credentials. CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog on 20 November alongside the vCenter zero-day. Cisco disclosed and fixed it on 21 October; there is no workaround. No OT victim is reported, but Expressway is a perimeter gateway that often bridges outside callers into internal networks, so an exposed, unpatched cluster is a foothold close to plant-side systems (editorial assessment).

items.title: Java4Shell exploitation attempts begin, and Siemens tells customers to take Industrial Edge Management offline until patched
items.content_text: Probing for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption bug in how OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later decode Base64 data, started within two days of its 17 November disclosure. GreyNoise counted more than 150 matching requests from five addresses by early 19 November and Previdian logged nine attempts from six addresses; none is confirmed to have succeeded. Exploitation needs a recent Intel or AMD x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, and researchers at Calif showed unauthenticated code execution against default Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Keycloak setups, each with a tailored chain. For OT teams the key item is Siemens advisory SSA-272816: three Industrial Edge Management products are affected, fixes are in progress, and Siemens recommends taking those instances offline until they are patched. Cisco lists more than a dozen products with no fix yet, and Atlassian Data Center products are also unpatched.

items.title: A Brotli flaw already in CISA’s exploited list turns up in Siemens WinCC, WinCC OA and BRAUMAT, and most products have no fix yet
items.content_text: Siemens says a widely used compression library flaw, CVE-2026-111497, reaches into several of its industrial software lines, and CISA republished the assessment as an ICS advisory on 17 November. The bug is an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder that can crash the software, leak information or possibly allow code execution. CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 27 October because of attacks elsewhere; nobody has reported exploitation through a Siemens product. Affected products named include BRAUMAT and SISTAR V8.2, WinCC OA V3.20 and V3.21, WinCC Runtime Professional, WinCC V7/V8 and TIA Administrator. Fixes exist only for BRAUMAT/SISTAR (V8.2 Update 5) and WinCC OA V3.20 (P17.1). WinCC OA is used as SCADA in grid control rooms, substations and renewable plants, so power operators should treat it as a priority while most sites rely on the workaround (editorial assessment).

items.title: Hitachi Energy TRO600 wireless routers let an unauthenticated attacker read configuration and password files; firmware 9.2.2.1 fixes it
items.content_text: CISA republished Hitachi Energy advisory 8DBD000224 on 29 October as ICSA-26-302-02; Hitachi Energy and the CVE records date it 27 October. It covers firmware for the TRO600 series, which Hitachi Energy describes as high-throughput, low-latency industrial wireless communications devices used by utilities, oil and gas companies and mining operators. CVE-2026-106087 (CVSS v3.1 7.5 in CISA’s advisory; v4.0 8.7 from Hitachi Energy) is missing authentication: an unauthenticated attacker can read or download arbitrary files on the device, including configuration files and password data, in firmware 9.1.1.0 and earlier. CVE-2026-10756 (v3.1 7.5; v4.0 7.7) lets an authenticated attacker use port forwarding to get past network access restrictions and reach services meant to be reachable only from the device itself, in 9.2.1.6 and earlier. Firmware 9.1.2.0 fixes the first flaw and 9.2.2.1 fixes both; Hitachi Energy recommends 9.2.2.1. The advisory’s summary mentions remote code execution, but neither flaw description does. CISA lists the Energy sector and reports no known exploitation. Configuration and password data taken from a field-network router could give an attacker the credentials and network layout to reach substations and other remote sites (editorial assessment).

items.title: Hitachi Energy CoreTec4 and CoreTec5: an authenticated command injection and a kernel root flaw with public exploit code; CoreTec4 owners must migrate
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-302-03, first released on 27 October and republished on 29 October from Hitachi Energy advisory 8DBD000258, covers CoreTec4 and CoreTec5 at 3.4.0 and earlier. Hitachi Energy says CoreTec technology powers its TXpert Hub monitoring system, part of its line for digitalizing transformers. CVE-2026-13162 (CVSS v3.1 7.5 in CISA’s advisory; v4.0 7.7 from Hitachi Energy) is an OS command injection in the configuration daemon’s time-zone handler: an authenticated user with certain roles can run arbitrary system commands and take full control. CoreTec5 is also affected by the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-43284, which lets a local low-privileged user become root; CISA’s assessment notes public proof-of-concept code, and the sources disagree on its score. CoreTec5 5.0.0 fixes both. CoreTec4 has no fixed version, and the remedy is migrating to CoreTec5 5.0.0. The CVE record for CVE-2026-13162 lists CoreTec5 up to 5.0.0 as affected, which conflicts with the advisory, so confirm the fixed version with Hitachi Energy. CISA lists the Energy sector and reports no known exploitation; neither flaw is in KEV, and the kernel flaw is a different one from CVE-2026-46300, which is. A compromised monitoring device on a substation network is a foothold beside protection and control equipment (editorial assessment).

items.title: AutomationDirect C-More EA9 HMI programming software can be taken over by a booby-trapped project file
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-328-01 (24 November) covers the C-More EA9 programming software that engineers use to build screens for AutomationDirect’s EA9 touch-panel HMIs. CVE-2026-127280 (CVSS 7.8) is a heap-based buffer overflow: opening a crafted project file in version 6.80 or earlier can let an attacker run code on the engineering workstation. CISA lists critical manufacturing, energy and water among the sectors using the product and reports no known exploitation. The risk is the engineering laptop, which often holds credentials and project files for many sites. Small generators, substations and plant balance-of-plant panels are where EA9 HMIs tend to turn up (editorial assessment).

items.title: DOE rules on barring grid equipment tied to covered foreign entities are due 24 December, and they could reach existing contracts
items.content_text: Executive Order 14421, signed on 26 August, lets the Energy Secretary prohibit buying, importing, transferring or installing foreign-produced bulk-power equipment tied to a “covered foreign entity”, at its core Chinese entities. A 27 October POWER Magazine analysis by Vinson & Elkins lawyers notes the prohibition applies notwithstanding existing contracts, and that DOE’s implementing rules, due by 24 December, will decide which equipment and manufacturers are covered and whether licences are available. DOE’s FAQ (updated 6 October) lists transformers, breakers, protective relays, generators, grid-connected inverters, battery storage and industrial control systems, and says associated software, firmware, remote access and services may count; foreign origin alone does not trigger a ban. Nothing is barred yet. For OT teams the practical step is an accurate inventory of installed and ordered control, protection and inverter equipment, and of who can reach it remotely (editorial assessment).
